extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, ML practitioners, and evaluators of large language models
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation guidelines and empirical tests for measuring an LLM's theory-of-mind, explainability (output- and process-consistency), and discriminative capabilities (e.g., PII detection, truthfulness). Includes prompt designs, test types, and limitations to consider when judging model behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Mind capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to reason about the mental states of others, handle multiple actors, and propose actions for cooperation toward common goals in social situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate using both basic and realistic scenarios (e.g., modernized Sally-Anne test, ZURFIN scenario). Test abstract and novel situations unlikely seen in training. Compare model outputs on reasoning about others' beliefs, intentions, and how actions change mental states. Note: GPT-4 outperforms earlier models on these dimensions in the paper's experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Mind limitations to test
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects of theory-of-mind not covered by the basic tests and therefore important to probe separately, e.g., understanding sarcasm, irony, humor, deception, and non-verbal cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design targeted tests for sarcasm/irony/humor/deception and multimodal/non-verbal cues (facial expressions, gestures, tone) where applicable; recognize that text-only tests do not capture full social interaction richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability — formal decomposition (PT and PE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the generation process as PT(y | x, c) (the process simulated to produce output y given input x and context c) and the explanatory process as PE(e | x, c, y) (the post-hoc explanation e for output y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing explanations, explicitly consider how x, c, and y shape both PT and PE. Prompt engineering aims to set (x, c) so PT approximates the task. PE can be customized via context c for different end users (e.g., child vs. researcher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Output-consistency of explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation is output-consistent if it is consistent with the output y given the input x and context c — i.e., it provides a plausible causal account of how y was derived from x and c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the explanation plausibly explains the specific generated output. Examples: GPT-4 often generates reasonable output-consistent explanations even for wrong answers (see Figures 6.7–6.9). Output-consistency is necessary but not sufficient for good explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-consistency of explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation is process-consistent if it is consistent with the model's simulated process PT — i.e., it permits making predictions about future model behavior under different inputs/contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test process-consistency by creating new inputs where the explanation should predict behavior (editing experiments, concept override experiments). Examples in the paper: changing symbol letters (P→R) or overriding alphabetical ordering to test whether the explanation predicts generation changes (Fig. 6.10). Process-consistency is stronger and harder to achieve than output-consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for testing explanation faithfulness (editing and concept-override experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental designs to probe whether an explanation truly reflects the model's internal simulation of PT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing experiment: change aspects of the original prompt (e.g., rename symbol from P to R) and observe prediction shifts; Concept override experiment: override model background knowledge in the prompt to see whether predicted outputs change (e.g., force a different alphabetical ordering). Use such experiments to distinguish output-consistency from process-consistency (Figures 6.10, 6.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that influence process-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Process-consistency can break down due to (1) poor/highly sensitive simulation of PT, (2) inherent arbitrariness/hard-to-explain tasks, (3) insufficient explanatory power of PE, or (4) the model's inability to simulate PE correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating explanations, consider whether PT is stable and explainable; for near-arbitrary choices (e.g., gender defaults in translation), expect weaker process-consistency. Reduce sensitivity by specifying PT in detail via richer context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and cautions for output-consistent explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Output-consistent explanations can provide reasonable accounts of how a prediction could have been made and thus offer insight, even when process-consistency is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educate users not to assume process-consistency from plausible explanations; encourage testing explanations for process-consistency. The model itself can help propose such tests (example: GPT-4 generating tests of its own explanation in Fig. 6.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination as a capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of an agent to make distinctions between different stimuli, concepts, and situations, enabling more accurate judgments and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess discriminative prowess across tasks such as identifying PII, ranking answers by closeness to a gold answer, and other classification-like judgements. Use datasets and specific tasks to quantify performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: PII detection task and evaluation buckets
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sentence, identify all personally identifiable information (PII) segments and count them. Evaluate performance by whether the model: (a) determines the exact number of PII elements, (b) misses one element, (c) misses two elements, or (d) misses more than two elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a labeled dataset (e.g., TAB subset) to derive ground-truth PII counts. Compare against specialized tools (example: Presidio). Report fraction exact, missing1, missing2, missing>2 as in Table 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: PII category rubric (explicit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories of information to treat as PII used in the prompt: (a) Names of people, including nicknames/aliases, usernames and initials; (b) Numbers and codes that identify something, such as SSN, phone number, passport number, license plate; (c) Places and locations, such as: cities, areas, countries, etc. or named infrastructures (bus stops, bridges, etc.); (d) Names of organisations, such as public and private companies schools, universities, public institutions, prisons, healthcare institutions non-governmental organisations, churches, etc.; (e) Demographic attribute of a person, such as native language, descent, heritage, ethnicity, job titles, ranks, education, physical descriptions, diagnosis, birthmarks, ages; (f) Description of a specific date (e.g., October 3, 2018), time (e.g., 9:48 AM) or duration (e.g., 18 years); (g) Description of a meaningful quantity, e.g., percentages and/or monetary values; (h) Every other type of information that describes an individual and that does not belong to the categories above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide these categories in the prompt (zero-shot or few-shot) to guide the model's enumerations. Use explicit output format constraints (e.g., return a python list labeled 'LIST:' and a 'COUNT:') to simplify evaluation and parsing (see Fig. 7.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt design for PII detection (zero-shot example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a zero-shot prompt that enumerates PII categories and instructs the model to list PII elements and count them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concrete instruction set improves performance even without examples. The paper's zero-shot prompt lists categories (a)-(h) and asks for LIST: and COUNT:. GPT-4, with this prompt, achieved 77.4% exact matches on the TAB subset versus 40.8% for Presidio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconceptions and fact-checking evaluation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate answers to open-world questions (TruthfulQA) and measure whether generated answers match gold answers; construct prompts with a preamble of Q/A examples followed by the target question to influence generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the TruthfulQA dataset and prompt the model with several question-answer exemplars in the preamble, then generate the completion for the target question (see Fig. 7.2). This setup serves both to create answers and to analyze truthfulness and similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of text-similarity metrics for truthfulness (and their limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common metrics used: ROUGE, BLEU, BLEURT; classify a generated completion as 'truthful' if similarity exceeds a pre-determined threshold against the gold answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics can show GPT-4 outputs closer to gold answers than prior models, but they are insufficient. Hedging (long, meandering answers) and paraphrasing reduce similarity scores even when the answer is accurate. Manual inspection is necessary for low-scoring but plausible outputs; consider alternative/robust truthfulness evaluations beyond surface n-gram overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompting strategy for truthfulness experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a preamble comprising several questions and their correct answers before the target question to steer the model's responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example preamble includes diverse Q/A pairs (factual and 'I have no comment' for nonsense queries) to set desired behavior. Evaluate how this preamble affects model correctness across categories and monitor for hedging-induced metric artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance for evaluation results
rubrics_metrics.description: When model-generated responses score poorly on automatic similarity metrics, differentiate between true inaccuracies and metric artifacts (e.g., hedging or longer helpful answers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform manual inspection on low-scoring examples to determine whether degradation is due to actual inaccuracy or verbose/hedged but accurate responses. Use this to refine evaluation thresholds or design complementary evaluation measures.
